title: Brand colour does not belong in your primitives
excerpt: Extracting brand into its own collection is thirty minutes of work that saves a rebuild the first time a client asks for their own palette.
authorBio: Design lead at Orvexiq Lab. Builds design systems and product interfaces for regulated businesses — mostly fintech and logistics.

body.text: Almost every design system I audit puts the brand blue in the primitive layer, named something like Color/Brand/Primary/500. It looks tidy. It is the single decision that makes the system impossible to reuse.

A primitive is a raw value with no opinion about where it is used. Blue/500 is a primitive. Brand/Primary/500 is not — the word "primary" is already a decision about role, and "brand" is already a decision about ownership. You have smuggled two layers of meaning into the layer that is supposed to have none.

This matters the moment you have a second brand. A client, a sub-product, a white-label deployment. If brand lives in primitives, every semantic token that points at it now points at something that has to change, and you are editing the foundation to serve one customer.

On a recent build we had 52 semantic tokens referencing the brand ramp from inside Primitives. The client asked, reasonably, whether their own palette could be swapped in without touching anything else. The honest answer at that point was no.
"If brand lives in your primitives, every client engagement becomes a fork of your foundation."

Pull the brand ramp out of Primitives into its own collection with a single mode. Repoint the semantic tokens at it. Primitives keep every hue as raw chromatic values; Brand holds only the ramp that carries identity; Semantics reference Brand, never the raw hue.

items: Primitives lose nothing — the hues were already there under Chromatic.
Brand becomes one collection you swap per client, per product, or per season.
Charts must never source from Brand, or every chart changes colour when the brand does.
A collection has exactly one mode axis, so brand, theme and density each need their own.

body.caption: Primitives hold raw hues. Brand holds only what carries identity. Semantics never reach past Brand.

body.text: On that build the migration was 52 references and took under an hour, with zero visual regression — the resolved values were identical, only the path changed. Doing it after the system had shipped to three products would have been a different afternoon entirely.
The rule I would give anyone starting: if a token name contains your company name, it does not belong in the foundation layer.
